cards.q: You need to know whether a function throws when its argument is empty. Which kind of document do you want?
cards.a: Reference: it describes every case precisely.

cards.q: You have never used a library and want to get something working. Where do you start?
cards.a: A tutorial, then the reference for the functions it uses.

cards.q: A forum answer says a function returns -1 on error. How should you treat that?
cards.a: As a lead to confirm on the function's reference page, for the version you are using.

cards.q: Why should a reference page not tell a story?
cards.a: Its job is to let readers find exact facts quickly; narrative hides them.

cards.q: You call `trim_left(s, "x")`. Which overload is used?
cards.a: (1): a string literal converts to `std::string_view`, not to `char`.

cards.q: What does `trim_left("xxx", "x")` return, according to the page?
cards.a: An empty string: every character is removed.

cards.q: What does "may throw `std::bad_alloc`" mean for your code?
cards.a: It can throw that exception, so code that must not fail has to be ready for it, even if it rarely happens.

cards.q: Which section should you always skim even when you think you have your answer?
cards.a: Notes (remarks): they hold the surprises and edge cases.

cards.q: A parameter is `std::vector<int>& out`. What does that tell you?
cards.a: The function writes to (or changes) your vector: it is an output or in-out parameter.

cards.q: Why does `std::sort` not compile on a `std::list`?
cards.a: It requires random-access iterators, and a list's iterators are only bidirectional.

cards.q: What does `[[nodiscard]]` on a function tell you?
cards.a: Its return value is important; ignoring it is almost certainly a bug.

cards.q: `std::map::insert` returns `std::pair<iterator, bool>`. What does the `bool` mean?
cards.a: Whether the element was inserted (false if the key was already there).

cards.q: A page says "`n` must be less than `size()`; otherwise the behaviour is undefined". Who is responsible for checking?
cards.a: You, before calling: the function does not check.

cards.q: A range is `[first, last)` with `first == last`. How many elements does it hold?
cards.a: None: it is empty.

cards.q: What is the difference between `v[i]` and `v.at(i)` for an index that is too large?
cards.a: `v[i]` is undefined behaviour; `v.at(i)` throws `std::out_of_range`.

cards.q: `push_back` gives the strong guarantee. What does that mean if it throws?
cards.a: The vector is exactly as it was before the call.

cards.q: Which is the final word on C++: cppreference or the standard?
cards.a: The standard; cppreference is a careful community reference that follows it.

cards.q: A member function is marked (C++20). Can you call it when compiling as C++17?
cards.a: No; it was added in C++20.

cards.q: Why not rely on a page's "possible implementation"?
cards.a: The real library may be implemented differently; only the documented behaviour is guaranteed.

cards.q: What does `std::stoi("  12abc", &used)` set `used` to?
cards.a: 4: two spaces and two digits were processed.

cards.q: `m.insert({"a", 5})` is called when `m["a"]` is already 1. What is `m["a"]` afterwards?
cards.a: Still 1: `insert` does nothing when the key exists.

cards.q: How do you know `std::from_chars` parsed the whole string?
cards.a: `ec` is `std::errc{}` and `ptr` equals the end of the input.

cards.q: When would you choose the `std::error_code&` overload of a filesystem function?
cards.a: When failure is an expected, normal outcome you want to handle without exceptions.

cards.q: What does `std::string::find` return when the text is not found?
cards.a: `std::string::npos`.

cards.q: What does "amortised constant" mean for `push_back`?
cards.a: Usually constant time, occasionally a costly reallocation, constant on average over many calls.

cards.q: You hold a reference to an element of a `std::map` and insert another element. Is the reference still valid?
cards.a: Yes: inserting into a map invalidates nothing.

cards.q: What is wrong with `v.erase(it); ++it;`?
cards.a: `it` is invalid after `erase`; use the iterator `erase` returns.

cards.q: Does `push_back` always invalidate every iterator of a vector?
cards.a: Only when it reallocates (size exceeds capacity); otherwise only `end()` changes.

cards.q: A member is marked (since C++20) and your project uses `/std:c++17`. What happens if you call it?
cards.a: It does not compile (it is not declared in C++17 mode).

cards.q: Why might `__cplusplus` say 199711L on MSVC even in C++20 mode?
cards.a: MSVC keeps the old value unless `/Zc:__cplusplus` is given; `_MSVC_LANG` has the real one.

cards.q: Where do you find a feature-test macro's name?
cards.a: In the Notes section of the feature's reference page (and the list of library feature-test macros).

cards.q: What does `std::format("[{:6}]", "ab")` produce?
cards.a: `[ab    ]`: strings align left by default.

cards.q: `nSize` is described as a size in characters. You have `wchar_t buffer[260]`. What do you pass?
cards.a: 260 (`std::size(buffer)`), not `sizeof(buffer)`, which is 520.

cards.q: `GetModuleFileNameW` returns exactly `nSize`. What happened?
cards.a: The buffer was too small and the path was truncated.

cards.q: What does a null `hModule` mean for this function?
cards.a: The executable file of the current process.

cards.q: What is the difference between the Library and DLL lines in the requirements?
cards.a: The library is what you link against at build time; the DLL is where the function is loaded from at run time.

cards.q: What does `_In_opt_` on a parameter tell you?
cards.a: The function only reads it, and null is allowed.

cards.q: A function takes `_Out_writes_bytes_(cb)`. You have a buffer of 50 `wchar_t`s. What do you pass as `cb`?
cards.a: 100 (50 × sizeof(wchar_t)), the size in bytes.

cards.q: `GetEnvironmentVariableW` returns 12 for a buffer of 10 characters. What does 12 mean?
cards.a: The buffer is too small; 12 characters, including the null, are needed.

cards.q: Why should a size-query-then-fetch sequence be a loop?
cards.a: The value may change between the calls and need a bigger buffer the second time.

cards.q: A function returns `S_FALSE`. Did it fail?
cards.a: No: `S_FALSE` is a success code (`SUCCEEDED` is true) meaning "no" or "nothing to do".

cards.q: What Win32 error is inside the HRESULT `0x80070002`?
cards.a: 2, `ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND` (facility 7 means Win32).

cards.q: A registry function returns 5. Should you call `GetLastError`?
cards.a: No: registry functions return the error code directly; 5 is `ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED`.

cards.q: What severity does the NTSTATUS `0xC0000005` have?
cards.a: Error: its top two bits are `11`.

cards.q: Why must you set `cbSize` before calling a function that takes the structure?
cards.a: It tells the function which version of the structure you have, so it reads and writes only those members.

cards.q: A page says "can be one of the following values". May you combine two with `|`?
cards.a: No: it takes a single value; combining gives a different, unintended value.

cards.q: What should you put in a member documented as "reserved; must be zero"?
cards.a: Zero; zero-initialising the whole structure with `{}` does it.

cards.q: What does `#define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0A00` do?
cards.a: Tells the Windows headers you target Windows 10, making declarations up to that version available.

cards.q: Can you call `sorted([3, 1], None, True)`?
cards.a: No: `key` and `reverse` come after `*`, so they are keyword-only.

cards.q: What does `"a,,b".split(",")` return, and how is that different from `"a  b".split()`?
cards.a: `['a', '', 'b']`; with no separator, runs of whitespace are one separator and empty strings are dropped, giving `['a', 'b']`.

cards.q: What does a "CPython implementation detail" note mean for your code?
cards.a: It describes the reference interpreter only; other implementations may differ, so do not rely on it.

cards.q: Why is `x = x.sort()` a bug?
cards.a: `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`, so `x` becomes `None`.

cards.q: What does `parseInt("12.5kg")` return?
cards.a: 12: it reads digits until the first character that is not one.
Without a compare function, elements are compared as strings.

cards.q: Should production code use an API marked Stability: 1?
cards.a: Better not: experimental APIs may change or be removed.

cards.q: Why compare `err.code` instead of `err.message` in Node?
cards.a: Codes are a documented, stable interface; message texts can change between versions.

cards.q: A function returns `const T*` and has no documentation. What can you assume about ownership?
cards.a: Nothing for certain, but most likely you do not own it and must not delete it; look for a comment, tests or the implementation to confirm how long it lives.

cards.q: `findInt` returns an empty optional. What two situations could that mean?
cards.a: The key is missing, or its value is not a complete integer.

cards.q: Why look at a project's tests when its docs are thin?
cards.a: They show intended usage and edge cases, and they match the code's real behaviour.

cards.q: You find in the source that a function happens to sort its output. May you rely on that?
cards.a: Not safely: it is not documented, so it may change; if you must, pin it with your own test.

cards.q: `man open` shows a shell command page. How do you get the system call?
cards.a: `man 2 open`: system calls are in section 2.

cards.q: A spec says senders SHOULD NOT send trailing whitespace. Must a receiver handle it?
cards.a: Yes: SHOULD NOT allows senders to do it with good reason, so a robust receiver must cope.

cards.q: What does `1*DIGIT` mean in ABNF?
cards.a: One or more digits.

cards.q: How do you find corrections to a published RFC?
cards.a: In its errata, and in any newer RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

cards.q: Why run an example unchanged before adapting it?
cards.a: To confirm it works in your environment, so later problems are known to come from your changes.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: An example calls `read` once. When is that not enough?
cards.a: When a read can return fewer bytes than requested: you must loop until the end.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: How do you make sure a handle is closed on every error path?
cards.a: Wrap it in an RAII object whose destructor closes it.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: What is wrong with `std::string(buffer, n)` when `n` can be -1?
cards.a: -1 converted to `size_t` is a huge length: it reads far past the buffer.
cards.lessonTitle: Turning an Example into Your Code

cards.q: Why write down a prediction before running an experiment?
cards.a: So you notice when the result surprises you, which is when you learn something.

cards.q: What does `std::nearbyint(2.5)` return by default, and why?
cards.a: 2.0: the default rounding mode rounds halves to the even neighbour.

cards.q: What is a learning test?
cards.a: A test that pins down a library's behaviour your code relies on, so a change is noticed when the library is upgraded.

cards.q: An experiment reading one element past the end of a vector prints 0. What have you learned?
cards.a: Nothing you can rely on: it is undefined behaviour, and it may do anything elsewhere.

cards.q: An example from the docs does not compile. What do you check first?
cards.a: Whether the docs and your installed version match.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: You upgrade a library from 1.4 to 3.1. Which changelog entries should you read?
cards.a: Every release between 1.4 and 3.1, especially the major versions 2.0 and 3.0.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: What makes a good documentation bug report?
cards.a: The page and section, what it says, what actually happens with a minimal program, and the version.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: How should you treat a function an AI assistant suggests?
cards.a: As a lead: confirm it exists and behaves as described on its reference page, then test it.
cards.lessonTitle: When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing

cards.q: Why should a doc comment say what a function does rather than how?
cards.a: So the implementation can change without making the documentation wrong, and readers get the contract they can rely on.

cards.q: A parameter is a timeout. What must its documentation include?
cards.a: Its unit (for example milliseconds) and the allowed values, including what 0 or a negative value means.

cards.q: What belongs in a changelog entry for a breaking change?
cards.a: What changed, what users must do about it, marked as breaking, in a new major version.

cards.q: How can tests help keep documentation true?
cards.a: Each documented behaviour, especially each error case, becomes a test, so a change that breaks the documentation fails the build.
